name: Bald Eagle
fact: Its nests are the largest built by any North American bird; one in Florida measured nearly 3 m across and weighed over two tonnes.

name: American Robin
fact: It hunts worms partly by sight, and the head-cocking pose is the bird lining up one eye on the ground.

name: Northern Cardinal
fact: Unusually for North American songbirds, the female sings too, often from the nest.

name: Blue Jay
fact: Its blue is a trick of light: the feathers contain no blue pigment, only structures that scatter blue wavelengths.

name: American Goldfinch
fact: It nests in late summer, timing its chicks to the seeding of thistles.

name: Ruby-throated Hummingbird
fact: Many cross the Gulf of Mexico in a single non-stop flight of around 800 km.

name: Wild Turkey
fact: Despite their bulk they roost in trees, and can burst into flight at around 90 km/h over short distances.

name: Mourning Dove
fact: The whistling sound at take-off comes from the wing feathers, not the voice.

name: Great Blue Heron
fact: Specialised neck vertebrae let it fold the neck into an S and strike like a released spring.

name: Canada Goose
fact: Goslings imprint on the first mover they see, a quirk exploited to teach captive-bred flocks migration routes behind microlight aircraft.

name: Snowy Owl
fact: Unlike most owls it hunts by day, an adaptation to Arctic summers with no night.

name: Great Horned Owl
fact: One of the few predators that routinely eats skunks, apparently untroubled by the spray.

name: Red-tailed Hawk
fact: Its rasping scream is dubbed over Bald Eagles in countless films, because the eagle's real call is a thin chatter.

name: American Crow
fact: Crows recognise individual human faces and will hold a grudge for years, passing the wariness to their offspring.

name: Northern Mockingbird
fact: A single male may learn 200 songs in a lifetime, including car alarms and creaking gates.

name: Black-capped Chickadee
fact: It adds dee notes to its call for more dangerous predators, so the alarm encodes threat size.

name: Downy Woodpecker
fact: The smallest woodpecker in North America, light enough to forage on weed stems.

name: Pileated Woodpecker
fact: It chisels rectangular holes so deep they can snap a small tree in half.

name: California Condor
fact: The wild population fell to zero in 1987 when the last 22 birds were taken into captivity; their descendants fly again over California.

name: Greater Roadrunner
fact: It runs at about 30 km/h and is one of the few animals that regularly kills rattlesnakes.

name: American White Pelican
fact: Groups herd fish into the shallows and scoop them up in unison rather than diving.

name: Sandhill Crane
fact: Fossils essentially identical to the modern bird are around 2.5 million years old.

name: Common Loon
fact: Its bones are unusually solid rather than hollow, which helps it dive but makes take-off a long taxi across the water.

name: Baltimore Oriole
fact: The female weaves a hanging pouch nest that can take a week and holds together for a full season of storms.

name: Red-winged Blackbird
fact: Males hide the red shoulder patches when feeding elsewhere, then flare them to claim a territory.

name: Eastern Bluebird
fact: The species rebounded from a steep decline largely thanks to volunteers installing nest-box trails.

name: Cedar Waxwing
fact: Flocks pass berries down a line beak to beak; birds gorging on fermented fruit can become visibly drunk.

name: Belted Kingfisher
fact: It nests at the end of a burrow the pair digs up to two metres into a river bank.

name: Wood Duck
fact: Ducklings leap from tree-hole nests up to 15 m up on their first day and bounce unhurt.

name: White-breasted Nuthatch
fact: It walks head-first down trunks, spotting food that upward-climbing birds miss.

name: Indigo Bunting
fact: It migrates at night and navigates by the rotation of the stars around the North Star.

name: Northern Flicker
fact: A woodpecker that mostly feeds on the ground, hammering into ant nests with a barbed tongue.

name: Killdeer
fact: It lures predators away by faking a broken wing, then flies off once the intruder is far enough from the nest.

name: Atlantic Puffin
fact: Backward-facing spines on its tongue and palate let it hold a dozen fish crosswise while still catching more.

name: Barn Owl
fact: Its ear openings sit at different heights, letting it pinpoint prey under snow or leaf litter in total darkness.

name: Osprey
fact: A reversible outer toe lets it carry fish head-first, cutting drag on the flight home.

name: Peregrine Falcon
fact: In a hunting stoop it exceeds 300 km/h, making it the fastest animal on Earth.

name: Rock Pigeon
fact: Homing pigeons sense the Earth's magnetic field and have carried messages through both world wars.

name: House Sparrow
fact: It has followed human settlement onto every continent except Antarctica.

name: Barn Swallow
fact: The most widespread swallow on Earth; European birds winter in southern Africa.

name: Common Starling
fact: Winter flocks form murmurations of hundreds of thousands that wheel as one without collisions.

name: Mallard
fact: Nearly every domestic duck breed except the Muscovy descends from this one species.

name: Great Egret
fact: Hunted almost to extinction for hat plumes, its recovery gave the National Audubon Society its emblem.

name: Cattle Egret
fact: It crossed the Atlantic unaided in the 1870s and spread through the Americas within a century.

name: Arctic Tern
fact: It migrates pole to pole each year, racking up roughly 70,000 km and more daylight than any other animal.

name: Common Raven
fact: Ravens solve multi-step puzzles, plan for future events, and appear to play purely for fun.

name: Turkey Vulture
fact: It finds carcasses by smell, an unusual skill among birds; gas engineers have used it to trace pipeline leaks.

name: Golden Eagle
fact: Kazakh and Mongolian falconers still hunt foxes and wolves with trained females.

name: Black Kite
fact: Australian kites have been recorded carrying burning sticks to spread grassfires and flush out prey.

name: European Robin
fact: It follows gardeners for the same reason it once followed wild boar: turned soil means exposed worms.

name: Common Blackbird
fact: Only the male is black; the female is a plain brown that often gets mistaken for another species.

name: Eurasian Blue Tit
fact: British blue tits famously learned to peck through foil milk-bottle tops, and the habit spread across the country.

name: Great Tit
fact: One of the most studied wild birds in the world; the Wytham Woods population has been tracked since 1947.

name: Eurasian Magpie
fact: It is one of the few non-mammals to pass the mirror mark test, suggesting self-recognition.

name: Common Chaffinch
fact: Males learn their song as youngsters, producing distinct regional dialects.

name: Mute Swan
fact: Among the heaviest flying birds; on the Thames they are still counted each year in the ceremony of swan upping.

name: Grey Heron
fact: It will stand motionless for many minutes before striking, and has been recorded taking rats and ducklings.

name: Common Kingfisher
fact: It must eat around its own body weight in fish daily, and a hard winter that freezes rivers can wipe out local populations.

name: European Goldfinch
fact: Its fine bill can extract teasel seeds that other finches cannot reach.

name: Eurasian Bullfinch
fact: Its taste for fruit-tree buds once made it a orchard pest with a bounty on its head in Britain.

name: Common Cuckoo
fact: Females lay in other birds' nests, and different lineages mimic the egg colour of their chosen host species.

name: White Stork
fact: A stork shot in Germany in 1822 carried an African spear through its neck, first proving birds migrated to Africa.

name: Common Swift
fact: Young birds can stay airborne for ten months without landing, eating, sleeping and mating on the wing.

name: Eurasian Eagle-Owl
fact: With a wingspan near 1.8 m it is among the largest owls, and takes prey as big as young foxes.

name: Tawny Owl
fact: The classic twit-twoo is a duet: the female calls and the male answers.

name: Northern Lapwing
fact: Its tumbling display flight and wavering call earned it the old country name peewit.

name: Eurasian Wren
fact: Tiny but astonishingly loud, it sings at about ten times the volume per gram of a crowing rooster.

name: Common Wood Pigeon
fact: Like all pigeons it feeds its young on crop milk, a protein-rich secretion produced by both parents.

name: Eurasian Jay
fact: A single bird may bury several thousand acorns each autumn, and the forgotten ones grow into oak woods.

name: Great Spotted Woodpecker
fact: Drumming is territorial signalling, not feeding, and can reach 20 strikes a second.

name: Northern Gannet
fact: It dives from 30 m at over 90 km/h, cushioned by air sacs beneath the skin of its face and chest.

name: European Herring Gull
fact: Chicks peck the red spot on the parent's bill to trigger feeding, a classic example of an innate releasing stimulus.

name: Common Kestrel
fact: It sees ultraviolet light, which makes vole urine trails glow as visible highways across a field.

name: Eurasian Hoopoe
fact: Nesting females produce a foul-smelling secretion that deters predators and coats the eggs with antimicrobials.

name: Red Kite
fact: Reduced to a handful of Welsh pairs by persecution, it is now one of Britain's great reintroduction successes.

name: Common Nightingale
fact: A drab brown bird with one of the most celebrated voices in European literature; only unpaired males sing at night.

name: Common Pheasant
fact: Native to Asia, it has been introduced for shooting so widely that most people meet it as a European farmland bird.

name: Common Ostrich
fact: The largest and heaviest living bird, it runs at 70 km/h and lays eggs weighing about 1.4 kg.

name: Secretarybird
fact: It kills snakes by stamping, delivering a kick with about five times its own body weight in force.

name: Grey Parrot
fact: Alex, a research bird, learned over 100 labels and appeared to grasp the concept of zero.

name: Grey Crowned Crane
fact: Alone among cranes it roosts in trees, thanks to a hind toe its relatives lack. It is Uganda's national bird.

name: Lilac-breasted Roller
fact: The name comes from the tumbling, rolling courtship dive the male performs from a high perch.

name: Southern Ground Hornbill
fact: It lives up to 70 years and breeds so slowly that a group raises roughly one surviving chick per decade.

name: Greater Flamingo
fact: The pink comes entirely from the diet; a flamingo fed differently fades to white.

name: Lesser Flamingo
fact: It breeds on caustic soda lakes hostile enough to burn human skin, which keeps predators away.

name: Marabou Stork
fact: Its wingspan rivals the albatross, and the bare head is an adaptation to feeding inside carcasses.

name: Shoebill
fact: It can stand motionless for hours, then collapse onto a lungfish in a strike known as the collapse.

name: Hamerkop
fact: Pairs build a domed stick nest up to 1.5 m across, strong enough to hold an adult human.

name: African Fish Eagle
fact: Its ringing call is so bound up with the continent's waterways that it is nicknamed the voice of Africa.

name: Hadada Ibis
fact: Named for its raucous haa-haa-de-dah call, delivered mostly while flying over suburban gardens at dawn.

name: Superb Starling
fact: It breeds cooperatively, with unrelated helpers raising chicks in long-running social groups.

name: Village Weaver
fact: The male knots a nest from strips of grass; if the female inspects it and disapproves, he tears it down and starts again.

name: Red-billed Quelea
fact: The most numerous wild bird on Earth, with flocks of millions that can strip a grain field in hours.

name: Helmeted Guineafowl
fact: Kept around farms as living alarm systems: they shriek at anything unfamiliar and eat ticks by the thousand.

name: Egyptian Goose
fact: Sacred to the ancient Egyptians and painted on tomb walls more than 4,000 years ago.

name: African Penguin
fact: Its braying call earned it the old name jackass penguin; the population has fallen by over 95% in a century.

name: Kori Bustard
fact: Often cited as the heaviest bird capable of flight, though it prefers to walk and takes off reluctantly.

name: Bateleur
fact: French for street performer, the name describes the rocking, tightrope-walker motion of its gliding flight.

name: Speckled Mousebird
fact: It creeps through foliage like a rodent and can hang upside down by one foot while feeding.

name: Ruppell's Vulture
fact: Holder of the highest confirmed bird flight: one struck an aircraft at 11,300 m over Ivory Coast.

name: Indian Peafowl
fact: The train is not the tail but greatly elongated upper tail coverts, moulted and regrown every year.

name: Red Junglefowl
fact: The wild ancestor of the domestic chicken, now the most numerous bird on the planet by a wide margin.

name: Mandarin Duck
fact: A symbol of marital devotion in China and Japan, often given to newlyweds as a pair.

name: Red-crowned Crane
fact: A symbol of luck and longevity in Japan; the red crown is bare skin that flushes brighter when the bird is excited.

name: Sarus Crane
fact: The tallest flying bird alive, standing up to 1.8 m, and famous in India for lifelong pair bonds.

name: Great Hornbill
fact: The female seals herself into a tree hollow with mud, leaving a slit through which the male feeds her for months.

name: Rose-ringed Parakeet
fact: Escaped cage birds have founded feral flocks as far north as London, Brussels and Tokyo.

name: Himalayan Monal
fact: The national bird of Nepal, it digs for tubers in alpine soil and can turn over hillsides of turf in a winter.

name: Golden Pheasant
fact: Native to the mountain forests of central China, though it is far better known from aviaries and parks.

name: Common Myna
fact: Introduced widely to control insects, it proved so successful at displacing native birds that it is now a listed invasive species.

name: House Crow
fact: It has hitched rides on ships to ports across the Middle East and Africa, arriving as an accidental stowaway.

name: Bar-headed Goose
fact: It crosses the Himalaya on migration, flying at altitudes where the air holds less than half the oxygen at sea level.

name: Steller's Sea Eagle
fact: The heaviest eagle in the world, with a bill so large it is visible in flight from a considerable distance.

name: Philippine Eagle
fact: The national bird of the Philippines; fewer than 400 pairs remain, each needing many square kilometres of forest.

name: Indian Roller
fact: Drab at rest, it flashes brilliant bands of blue the instant it opens its wings.

name: White-throated Kingfisher
fact: Despite the name it often hunts far from water, taking lizards and large insects from farmland perches.

name: Eurasian Tree Sparrow
fact: Targeted in China's 1958 Four Pests campaign; the resulting insect explosion contributed to catastrophic crop failures.

name: Andean Condor
fact: With a 3.2 m wingspan it can soar for over 150 km without a single flap.

name: Scarlet Macaw
fact: Flocks gather at riverbank clay licks, apparently to neutralise toxins in the unripe seeds they eat.

name: Blue-and-yellow Macaw
fact: Pairs fly so close their wingtips nearly touch, and they can live over 50 years.

name: Hyacinth Macaw
fact: The largest flying parrot, with a bill strong enough to crack palm nuts a person cannot open with a hammer.

name: Toco Toucan
fact: The huge bill is a radiator: the bird dumps body heat through it, adjusting blood flow like a thermostat.

name: Hoatzin
fact: It ferments leaves in a chambered crop like a cow, which makes it smell so bad locals call it the stinkbird.

name: Harpy Eagle
fact: Its rear talons are about the size of a grizzly bear's claws, and it plucks monkeys straight out of the canopy.

name: Andean Cock-of-the-rock
fact: Males gather at leks to bow, bounce and squawk while females walk the line and choose.

name: Greater Rhea
fact: The male incubates the eggs of several females in one nest and raises the chicks alone.

name: Magellanic Penguin
fact: It returns to the same burrow and the same mate year after year, recognising the partner by voice.

name: Chilean Flamingo
fact: It feeds in high Andean salt lakes that freeze overnight, standing in brine at nearly 4,500 m.

name: Sword-billed Hummingbird
fact: The only bird with a bill longer than its body; it must preen with its feet because the bill cannot reach.

name: Resplendent Quetzal
fact: Sacred to the Maya and Aztecs, who took the tail plumes without killing the bird; it gives Guatemala its currency name.

name: Keel-billed Toucan
fact: Belize's national bird sleeps in tree holes with its tail folded flat over its back and its bill tucked under a wing.

name: Jabiru
fact: The tallest flying bird in the Americas; the bare neck flushes scarlet when the bird is agitated.

name: Rufous Hornero
fact: Argentina's national bird builds a domed mud nest that bakes hard as pottery in the sun.

name: Burrowing Owl
fact: It nests underground and lines the tunnel with dung, which draws in the beetles it then eats.

name: Inca Tern
fact: Both sexes sport a white handlebar moustache, and its length signals the bird's health to mates.

name: Oilbird
fact: It roosts in pitch-dark caves and navigates by echolocation, clicking like a bat.

name: Blue-footed Booby
fact: The blue comes from dietary pigments, so a male high-stepping in courtship is advertising how well he has been eating.

name: Medium Ground Finch
fact: One of Darwin's finches; researchers on Daphne Major measured its beak evolving measurably within a single drought.

name: King Vulture
fact: It lets smaller vultures find the carcass, then displaces them, its stronger bill opening hides they cannot tear.

name: Scarlet Ibis
fact: The national bird of Trinidad and Tobago; chicks are drab grey and redden only as they take up a diet of red crabs.

name: Emu
fact: The second-tallest living bird. In 1932 Australia deployed soldiers with machine guns against them and effectively lost.

name: Southern Cassowary
fact: Its inner toe carries a dagger-like claw up to 12 cm long, and it is often called the world's most dangerous bird.

name: Southern Brown Kiwi
fact: Alone among birds it has nostrils at the bill tip, and it lays an egg up to a quarter of the female's body weight.

name: Kea
fact: The world's only alpine parrot, notorious for stripping the rubber from car windscreens purely out of curiosity.

name: Kakapo
fact: A flightless nocturnal parrot whose entire population is small enough that every living bird has a name.

name: Laughing Kookaburra
fact: The dawn chorus of cackling is a family territorial call, and the bird is a kingfisher that rarely touches water.

name: Sulphur-crested Cockatoo
fact: Sydney birds taught each other to flip wheelie-bin lids, and the technique spread suburb by suburb.

name: Galah
fact: So familiar in Australia that its name doubles as slang for a fool, despite the bird being notably clever.

name: Rainbow Lorikeet
fact: Its tongue ends in a brush of fine hairs for mopping nectar out of blossom.

name: Budgerigar
fact: Wild flocks in the outback can number tens of thousands and move wherever rain has fallen.

name: Superb Lyrebird
fact: It mimics whatever it hears, and wild birds have been recorded reproducing chainsaws and camera shutters.

name: Australian Magpie
fact: Its warbling carol is one of the most complex songs of any bird, and spring swooping is a strictly seasonal habit.

name: Black Swan
fact: Europeans assumed all swans were white until 1697, which is why the bird now names the black swan theory.

name: Little Penguin
fact: The smallest penguin at about 33 cm; colonies come ashore only after dark in a nightly penguin parade.

name: Tui
fact: It has two voice boxes and sings notes above human hearing, so part of its song registers only as silence.

name: Wedge-tailed Eagle
fact: Australia's largest raptor soars to 2,000 m and holds a territory it patrols for decades.

name: Greater Bird-of-paradise
fact: Early skins reached Europe with the feet removed, prompting the belief the birds never landed; apoda means footless.

name: Zebra Finch
fact: The main songbird model in neuroscience, because males learn their song from a tutor much as infants learn speech.

name: Willie Wagtail
fact: It fans and swings its tail constantly to flush insects, and will harass birds many times its size.

name: Australian White Ibis
fact: Driven from drying inland wetlands into the cities, where its bin-raiding earned it the nickname bin chicken.

name: Cockatiel
fact: The smallest cockatoo, and the only one whose males reliably learn to whistle tunes in captivity.

name: Wandering Albatross
fact: The largest wingspan of any living bird at 3.5 m; it circles the Southern Ocean and can glide for hours without flapping.

name: Emperor Penguin
fact: Males incubate a single egg on their feet through the Antarctic winter, fasting for around 65 days in -40C darkness.

name: Adelie Penguin
fact: It builds a nest of pebbles, and neighbours routinely steal from each other's piles.

name: Gentoo Penguin
fact: The fastest underwater bird, hitting 36 km/h in pursuit of fish.

name: Chinstrap Penguin
fact: Nesting birds sleep in bursts of about four seconds, thousands of times a day, to guard the nest continuously.

name: King Penguin
fact: Its chick takes over a year to fledge and wears a thick brown down once mistaken for a separate species.

name: Snow Petrel
fact: One of only three birds ever recorded breeding at the South Pole, nesting on bare rock far inland.

name: South Polar Skua
fact: A pirate that chases other seabirds until they drop their catch, and has been sighted at the South Pole itself.
